meaning: as for; marks the topic of the sentence
usage: Written は but pronounced 'wa'. It sets up what the sentence is about; the key information comes after it.

examples.japanese: 私は学生です。
examples.english: I am a student.

examples.japanese: 今日は天気がいいです。
examples.english: The weather is nice today.

examples.japanese: この本はおもしろいです。
examples.english: This book is interesting.

meaning: marks the subject; points out new or focused information
usage: Question words such as だれ and 何 take が, never は, when they are the subject. が is also used with 好き, ほしい, 上手 and わかる for the thing liked, wanted or understood.

examples.japanese: 雨が降っています。
examples.english: It is raining.

examples.japanese: だれが窓を開けましたか。
examples.english: Who opened the window?

examples.japanese: 私が行きます。
examples.english: I'll be the one to go.

meaning: marks the direct object of a verb; marks a place moved through or left
usage: Written を but pronounced 'o'. With movement verbs such as 歩く, 散歩する and 出る it marks the route or the place being left.

examples.japanese: 毎朝パンを食べます。
examples.english: I eat bread every morning.

examples.japanese: 姉は新しいかばんを買いました。
examples.english: My older sister bought a new bag.

examples.japanese: 公園を散歩しました。
examples.english: I took a walk in the park.

meaning: at; on; in (a specific point in time)
usage: Used with clock times, dates, days of the week and months. Relative words such as 今日, 明日, 毎日 and 来週 take no に.

examples.japanese: 毎朝7時に起きます。
examples.english: I get up at seven every morning.

examples.japanese: 日曜日に友達と会います。
examples.english: I'm meeting a friend on Sunday.

examples.japanese: 8月に国へ帰ります。
examples.english: I'm going back to my country in August.

structure: Noun + に + 行く / 来る / 帰る
usage: Close in meaning to へ. に puts the focus on the arrival point, へ on the direction.

examples.japanese: 毎日バスで学校に行きます。
examples.english: I go to school by bus every day.

examples.japanese: 夜10時に家に帰りました。
examples.english: I got home at 10 p.m.

examples.japanese: 来月、姉が日本に来ます。
examples.english: My older sister is coming to Japan next month.

meaning: in; at; on (where someone or something is)
structure: Noun + に + ある / いる
usage: Used with ある, いる and 住む. For the place where an action happens (eat, study, play), use で instead.

examples.japanese: 机の上に辞書があります。
examples.english: There is a dictionary on the desk.

examples.japanese: 姉は東京に住んでいます。
examples.english: My older sister lives in Tokyo.

examples.japanese: 猫は今どこにいますか。
examples.english: Where is the cat now?

meaning: to (the person who receives or is the target of an action)
usage: Common with あげる, 貸す, 教える, 見せる, 電話をかける and 会う. With もらう and 借りる, に marks the person you get something from.

examples.japanese: 母に手紙を書きます。
examples.english: I'm going to write a letter to my mother.

examples.japanese: 妹に本を貸しました。
examples.english: I lent a book to my younger sister.

examples.japanese: 友達に電話をかけました。
examples.english: I called my friend.

meaning: per; in (how many times within a period)
usage: The period comes first, then に, then the number of times: 月に一回 (once a month).

examples.japanese: 一週間に二回、プールで泳ぎます。
examples.english: I swim in the pool twice a week.

examples.japanese: 母は一日に二回、犬の散歩をします。
examples.english: My mother walks the dog twice a day.

examples.japanese: 一年に一度、家族で旅行します。
examples.english: Once a year, my family goes on a trip.

usage: Written へ but pronounced 'e'. Usually interchangeable with に for destinations; へ stresses the direction a little more.

examples.japanese: 夏休みに北海道へ行きます。
examples.english: I'm going to Hokkaido during summer vacation.

examples.japanese: 来週、国へ帰ります。
examples.english: I'm going back to my home country next week.

examples.japanese: どこへ行きますか。
examples.english: Where are you going?

meaning: at; in (the place where an action happens)
usage: Compare 教室にいます (being somewhere: に) with 教室で勉強します (doing something there: で).

examples.japanese: 図書館で本を読みます。
examples.english: I read books at the library.

examples.japanese: きのう、デパートでくつを買いました。
examples.english: Yesterday I bought shoes at the department store.

examples.japanese: 駅の前で友達を待ちました。
examples.english: I waited for my friend in front of the station.

meaning: by; with; in (means, tool, method or language)
usage: To say 'on foot', use 歩いて行きます rather than で.

examples.japanese: 毎日電車で会社へ行きます。
examples.english: I go to work by train every day.

examples.japanese: はしでご飯を食べます。
examples.english: I eat my meals with chopsticks.

examples.japanese: 日本語で手紙を書きました。
examples.english: I wrote a letter in Japanese.

meaning: and (joining nouns in a complete list)
usage: と lists every item; to give just some examples, use や. It joins nouns only, not verbs or adjectives.

examples.japanese: かばんの中にペンとノートがあります。
examples.english: There is a pen and a notebook in my bag.

examples.japanese: 朝ご飯にパンとたまごを食べました。
examples.english: I had bread and eggs for breakfast.

examples.japanese: 父と母は銀行で働いています。
examples.english: My father and mother work at a bank.

meaning: with; together with (a partner in an action)
usage: Often followed by いっしょに. With verbs like 話す, 会う and 結婚する, と marks the other person.

examples.japanese: 週末、友達と映画を見ました。
examples.english: I saw a movie with a friend on the weekend.

examples.japanese: 妹といっしょに買い物に行きます。
examples.english: I'm going shopping with my younger sister.

examples.japanese: だれと昼ご飯を食べましたか。
examples.english: Who did you have lunch with?

meaning: and (giving some examples out of more); ... and so on
usage: Suggests the list is not complete. Often ends with など: 本や雑誌など.

examples.japanese: 机の上に本や雑誌があります。
examples.english: On the desk there are books, magazines and so on.

examples.japanese: スーパーで肉や野菜を買いました。
examples.english: I bought meat, vegetables and other things at the supermarket.

usage: Means one of the items is chosen. To list items together, use と or や.

examples.japanese: 飲み物はコーヒーか紅茶がいいです。
examples.english: For a drink, coffee or tea would be good.

examples.japanese: 土曜日か日曜日に買い物に行きます。
examples.english: I'll go shopping on Saturday or Sunday.

examples.japanese: 駅までバスかタクシーで行きます。
examples.english: I'll go to the station by bus or taxi.

meaning: also; too; (with a negative) not ... either; neither ... nor
usage: も replaces は, が and を, but comes after other particles: 京都にも行きました.

examples.japanese: 私も学生です。
examples.english: I'm a student too.

examples.japanese: 兄はサッカーも好きです。
examples.english: My older brother likes soccer too.

examples.japanese: 肉も魚も食べません。
examples.english: I eat neither meat nor fish.

usage: The first noun describes the second: 日本の車 (a Japanese car). The second noun can be dropped when clear: それは私のです.

examples.japanese: これは私のかさです。
examples.english: This is my umbrella.

examples.japanese: 日本語の先生はとてもやさしいです。
examples.english: The Japanese teacher is very kind.

examples.japanese: 駅の近くに新しい店があります。
examples.english: There is a new shop near the station.

meaning: from (a starting point in time or place)
usage: Often paired with まで: 月曜日から金曜日まで (from Monday to Friday).

examples.japanese: 授業は9時からです。
examples.english: Class starts at nine.

examples.japanese: 学校から駅まで歩きます。
examples.english: I walk from school to the station.

examples.japanese: 私はブラジルから来ました。
examples.english: I'm from Brazil.

meaning: until; up to; as far as
usage: Marks the end point of something that continues. For a deadline ('by'), use までに (N4).

examples.japanese: 昼休みは1時までです。
examples.english: Lunch break is until one o'clock.

examples.japanese: 駅までいっしょに行きましょう。
examples.english: Let's go together as far as the station.

examples.japanese: きのうは夜11時まで勉強しました。
examples.english: Yesterday I studied until 11 p.m.

meaning: (question marker) turns a sentence into a question
usage: Polite questions end in か and are usually written with 。. In casual speech か is normally dropped and rising intonation is used instead.

examples.japanese: これはあなたのかばんですか。
examples.english: Is this your bag?

examples.japanese: 朝ご飯を食べましたか。
examples.english: Did you eat breakfast?

examples.japanese: トイレはどこですか。
examples.english: Where is the restroom?

meaning: isn't it?; right? (seeking agreement or sharing a feeling)
usage: Used when the speaker expects the listener to share the same view or knowledge. Compare よ, which tells the listener something new.

examples.japanese: 今日は暑いですね。
examples.english: It's hot today, isn't it?

examples.japanese: このケーキ、おいしいですね。
examples.english: This cake is delicious, isn't it?

examples.japanese: 明日のテストは10時からですね。
examples.english: Tomorrow's test starts at ten, right?

meaning: you know; I tell you (giving new information or emphasis)
usage: Tells the listener something they may not know. Overusing it with superiors can sound pushy.

examples.japanese: このラーメンはとてもおいしいですよ。
examples.english: This ramen is really good, you know.

examples.japanese: かさを忘れていますよ。
examples.english: You're forgetting your umbrella.

examples.japanese: 明日はテストがありますよ。
examples.english: There's a test tomorrow, you know.

usage: In X は Y より + adjective, Y is the standard. Japanese adjectives have no '-er' form; より does that job.

examples.japanese: 今日はきのうより寒いです。
examples.english: Today is colder than yesterday.

examples.japanese: 電車はバスより速いです。
examples.english: Trains are faster than buses.

examples.japanese: 兄は父より背が高いです。
examples.english: My older brother is taller than my father.

structure: Noun + の方が + Noun + より
usage: The two parts can come in either order. Often used to answer a どちら question.

examples.japanese: 犬の方が猫より好きです。
examples.english: I like dogs more than cats.

examples.japanese: 東京の方が大阪より人が多いです。
examples.english: Tokyo has more people than Osaka.

examples.japanese: 夏より冬の方が好きです。
examples.english: I like winter better than summer.

meaning: which is more ..., X or Y?
structure: Noun + と + Noun + とどちらが
usage: Compares exactly two things. どっち is the casual form of どちら. Answer with 〜の方が.

examples.japanese: コーヒーと紅茶とどちらが好きですか。
examples.english: Which do you like better, coffee or tea?

examples.japanese: 電車とバスとどちらが安いですか。
examples.english: Which is cheaper, the train or the bus?

examples.japanese: 「山と海とどちらがいいですか。」「海の方がいいです。」
examples.english: "Which is better, the mountains or the sea?" "The sea is better."

structure: Noun + の中で + Noun + が一番
usage: Used for three or more items. In questions use 何, だれ, どこ or いつ before が一番.

examples.japanese: 果物の中でりんごが一番好きです。
examples.english: Of all fruits, I like apples the most.

examples.japanese: クラスの中でだれが一番背が高いですか。
examples.english: Who is the tallest in the class?

examples.japanese: 家族の中で父が一番早く起きます。
examples.english: In my family, my father gets up the earliest.

structure: Noun + です / na-Adj + です / i-Adj + です
usage: Forms: です, ではありません, でした, ではありませんでした. After an い-adjective, です only adds politeness: 高いです.

examples.japanese: 私はマリアです。
examples.english: I'm Maria.

examples.japanese: 今日は月曜日です。
examples.english: Today is Monday.

examples.japanese: この部屋はとても静かです。
examples.english: This room is very quiet.

usage: Forms: だ, じゃない, だった, じゃなかった. Never used right after an い-adjective (高いだ is wrong). Often dropped in casual questions: 学生？

examples.japanese: 今日は日曜日だ。
examples.english: Today is Sunday.

examples.japanese: あの人は私の兄だ。
examples.english: That person is my older brother.

examples.japanese: 明日は休みだから、ゆっくり寝る。
examples.english: Tomorrow is a day off, so I'll sleep in.

meaning: is not; am not; are not
structure: Noun + ではありません / na-Adj + ではありません / Noun + じゃない / na-Adj + じゃない
usage: じゃありません and じゃないです are more conversational polite forms. Past: ではありませんでした / じゃなかった. い-adjectives use 〜くない instead.

examples.japanese: 私は先生ではありません。学生です。
examples.english: I'm not a teacher. I'm a student.

examples.japanese: 今日は休みじゃない。
examples.english: Today isn't a day off.

examples.japanese: この町はあまりにぎやかではありません。
examples.english: This town isn't very lively.

structure: Noun + でした / na-Adj + でした
usage: Past negative: ではありませんでした. い-adjectives do not take でした: say 高かったです, not 高いでした.

examples.japanese: きのうは私の誕生日でした。
examples.english: Yesterday was my birthday.

examples.japanese: 子どものころ、野菜がきらいでした。
examples.english: When I was a child, I didn't like vegetables.

examples.japanese: テストはかんたんでした。
examples.english: The test was easy.

meaning: polite non-past verb ending (do; will do)
usage: Covers habits and future actions. 飲む→飲みます, 食べる→食べます, する→します, 来る→来ます.

examples.japanese: 毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。
examples.english: I drink coffee every morning.

examples.japanese: 明日、京都へ行きます。
examples.english: I'm going to Kyoto tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 弟は毎晩9時に寝ます。
examples.english: My younger brother goes to bed at nine every night.

usage: The plain equivalent is the ない-form: 飲みません = 飲まない.

examples.japanese: 私はお酒を飲みません。
examples.english: I don't drink alcohol.

examples.japanese: 日曜日は学校へ行きません。
examples.english: I don't go to school on Sundays.

examples.japanese: 今晩はテレビを見ません。
examples.english: I won't watch TV tonight.

usage: The plain equivalent is the た-form: 会いました = 会った.

examples.japanese: きのう、友達に会いました。
examples.english: I met a friend yesterday.

examples.japanese: 先週、新しいくつを買いました。
examples.english: I bought new shoes last week.

examples.japanese: けさ、6時に起きました。
examples.english: I got up at six this morning.

usage: The plain equivalent is 〜なかった: 食べませんでした = 食べなかった.

examples.japanese: けさは朝ご飯を食べませんでした。
examples.english: I didn't eat breakfast this morning.

examples.japanese: 週末は宿題をしませんでした。
examples.english: I didn't do my homework over the weekend.

examples.japanese: きのうは雨でしたから、出かけませんでした。
examples.english: It rained yesterday, so I didn't go out.

meaning: do not; will not (plain negative of verbs)
usage: う-verbs change the last -u sound to -a: 書く→書かない, 買う→買わない. る-verbs drop る: 食べない. する→しない, 来る→こない, ある→ない. Past: 〜なかった.

examples.japanese: 今日は学校へ行かない。
examples.english: I'm not going to school today.

examples.japanese: 兄は肉を食べない。
examples.english: My older brother doesn't eat meat.

examples.japanese: 「コーヒー、飲む？」「ううん、飲まない。」
examples.english: "Are you having coffee?" "No, I'm not."

usage: Made exactly like the て-form, with て→た and で→だ: 書いて→書いた, 飲んで→飲んだ, 行って→行った. Polite equivalent: 〜ました.

examples.japanese: 週末は家で映画を見た。
examples.english: I watched a movie at home over the weekend.

examples.japanese: 駅で先生に会った。
examples.english: I ran into my teacher at the station.

examples.japanese: 「昼ご飯、食べた？」「うん、もう食べた。」
examples.english: "Did you eat lunch?" "Yeah, I already ate."

usage: Used when the speaker expects the listener to agree. To invite more gently, use 〜ませんか.

examples.japanese: いっしょに行きましょう。
examples.english: Let's go together.

examples.japanese: 少し休みましょう。
examples.english: Let's take a short break.

examples.japanese: 駅の前で会いましょう。
examples.english: Let's meet in front of the station.

usage: Offers to do something for the listener (shall I?) or asks them to decide something together (shall we?).

examples.japanese: 窓を開けましょうか。
examples.english: Shall I open the window?

examples.japanese: 荷物を持ちましょうか。
examples.english: Shall I carry your bags?

examples.japanese: 何時に会いましょうか。
examples.english: What time shall we meet?

meaning: won't you ...?; would you like to ...? (polite invitation)
usage: Gentler than 〜ましょう because it leaves the listener room to decline. Accept with ええ、〜ましょう.

examples.japanese: いっしょに昼ご飯を食べませんか。
examples.english: Would you like to have lunch together?

examples.japanese: 日曜日にテニスをしませんか。
examples.english: Would you like to play tennis on Sunday?

examples.japanese: 明日、公園を散歩しませんか。
examples.english: How about a walk in the park tomorrow?

usage: Conjugates like an い-adjective: 〜たくない, 〜たかった. The object can take が or を. Not used to state another person's wishes directly.

examples.japanese: 夏休みに沖縄へ行きたいです。
examples.english: I want to go to Okinawa during summer vacation.

examples.japanese: 冷たい水が飲みたいです。
examples.english: I want to drink some cold water.

examples.japanese: 何が食べたいですか。
examples.english: What do you want to eat?

usage: For things, not actions (actions use 〜たい). Conjugates like an い-adjective: ほしくない, ほしかった.

examples.japanese: 新しいパソコンがほしいです。
examples.english: I want a new computer.

examples.japanese: 誕生日に何がほしいですか。
examples.english: What do you want for your birthday?

examples.japanese: 今は何もほしくないです。
examples.english: I don't want anything right now.

usage: Used when shopping or ordering. A quantity goes after を with no particle: 切手を二枚ください.

examples.japanese: すみません、水をください。
examples.english: Excuse me, could I have some water?

examples.japanese: このりんごを三つください。
examples.english: I'll take three of these apples, please.

examples.japanese: メニューをください。
examples.english: Could I have the menu, please?

usage: Polite, but still an instruction the speaker expects to be followed. Softer requests use 〜てくれませんか (N4).

examples.japanese: もう少しゆっくり話してください。
examples.english: Please speak a little more slowly.

examples.japanese: ここでくつをぬいでください。
examples.english: Please take off your shoes here.

examples.japanese: すみません、駅までの道を教えてください。
examples.english: Excuse me, could you tell me the way to the station?

usage: Softer than 〜てはいけません. In casual speech ください is dropped: 見ないで.

examples.japanese: 教室で食べないでください。
examples.english: Please don't eat in the classroom.

examples.japanese: この部屋に入らないでください。
examples.english: Please don't go into this room.

examples.japanese: 心配しないでください。
examples.english: Please don't worry.

usage: Add ですか to ask for permission. A polite refusal is often just すみません、ちょっと….

examples.japanese: この辞書を使ってもいいですか。
examples.english: May I use this dictionary?

examples.japanese: 今日は早く帰ってもいいです。
examples.english: You may go home early today.

examples.japanese: ここにすわってもいいですか。
examples.english: Is it all right if I sit here?

usage: A strong prohibition, often for rules. Polite form: 〜てはいけません. Casual contraction: 〜ちゃいけない / 〜じゃいけない.

examples.japanese: 図書館で大きい声で話してはいけません。
examples.english: You must not talk loudly in the library.

examples.japanese: 子どもはこの川で泳いではいけません。
examples.english: Children must not swim in this river.

examples.japanese: ここでたばこを吸ってはいけません。
examples.english: You must not smoke here.

pattern: 〜なければならない / 〜なくてはいけない
structure: Verb-nai stem + なければならない / Verb-nai stem + なくてはいけない
usage: Polite forms end in なりません / いけません. The two mean the same; なければならない sounds slightly more formal.

examples.japanese: 明日は6時に起きなければなりません。
examples.english: I have to get up at six tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 今日は早く家に帰らなくてはいけません。
examples.english: I have to go home early today.

examples.japanese: 日本では、家に入る前にくつをぬがなければなりません。
examples.english: In Japan, you have to take off your shoes before going into a house.

structure: Verb-nai stem + なくてもいい
usage: The opposite of 〜なければならない. Ask with 〜なくてもいいですか (Is it all right if I don't ...?).

examples.japanese: 明日は学校へ来なくてもいいです。
examples.english: You don't have to come to school tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 名前は書かなくてもいいです。
examples.english: You don't need to write your name.

examples.japanese: 今日は料理をしなくてもいいですよ。
examples.english: You don't have to cook today.

meaning: be doing (ongoing action); be in a state (result of a change); do regularly
usage: With action verbs (食べる, 読む) it shows an action in progress; with change verbs (結婚する, 開く, 知る) it shows the resulting state. Polite: 〜ています.

examples.japanese: 弟は今、部屋でゲームをしています。
examples.english: My younger brother is playing a game in his room now.

examples.japanese: 姉は結婚しています。
examples.english: My older sister is married.

examples.japanese: 窓が開いています。
examples.english: The window is open.

meaning: and; and then (linking actions in order)
usage: The final verb sets the tense for the whole sentence. 書く→書いて, 飲む→飲んで, 話す→話して, 買う→買って, 行く→行って (irregular).

examples.japanese: 朝起きて、顔を洗います。
examples.english: I get up in the morning and wash my face.

examples.japanese: デパートへ行って、セーターを買いました。
examples.english: I went to the department store and bought a sweater.

examples.japanese: 家に帰って、晩ご飯を食べて、寝ました。
examples.english: I went home, ate dinner and went to bed.

meaning: after doing; (do A) and then (B); since
usage: Stresses that A is finished before B starts, more clearly than a plain て. With ている in the main clause it often means 'since'.

examples.japanese: 手を洗ってから、ご飯を食べましょう。
examples.english: Let's wash our hands and then eat.

examples.japanese: 宿題をしてから、テレビを見ます。
examples.english: I'll watch TV after I do my homework.

examples.japanese: 日本に来てから、毎日日本語を勉強しています。
examples.english: Since coming to Japan, I've been studying Japanese every day.

meaning: do things like A and B; sometimes A, sometimes B
structure: Verb-ta + り + Verb-ta + りする
usage: Picks out a few actions from many. Tense and politeness go on the final する: 〜たりしました.

examples.japanese: 日曜日はそうじをしたり、洗濯をしたりします。
examples.english: On Sundays I do things like cleaning and laundry.

examples.japanese: 休みの日は本を読んだり、音楽を聞いたりします。
examples.english: On my days off I read books, listen to music and so on.

examples.japanese: 夏休みは海で泳いだり、山に登ったりしました。
examples.english: During summer vacation I swam in the sea, climbed mountains and so on.

meaning: have (ever) done; have the experience of doing
usage: Talks about life experience, not something just done: きのう食べたことがある is wrong. Negative 〜たことがありません means 'have never'.

examples.japanese: 富士山に登ったことがあります。
examples.english: I have climbed Mt. Fuji.

examples.japanese: 日本の映画を見たことがありますか。
examples.english: Have you ever seen a Japanese movie?

examples.japanese: 私は馬に乗ったことがありません。
examples.english: I have never ridden a horse.

structure: Verb-dict + 前に / Noun + の + 前に
usage: The verb before 前に is always in dictionary form, even when talking about the past. With a length of time there is no の: 3年前に (three years ago).

examples.japanese: 寝る前に歯をみがきます。
examples.english: I brush my teeth before going to bed.

examples.japanese: 授業の前にコーヒーを飲みます。
examples.english: I drink coffee before class.

examples.japanese: 3年前に日本へ来ました。
examples.english: I came to Japan three years ago.

structure: Verb-ta + 後で / Noun + の + 後で
usage: The verb before 後で is always in た-form, even for future plans. On its own, 後で means 'later'.

examples.japanese: 晩ご飯を食べた後で、散歩をします。
examples.english: I take a walk after eating dinner.

examples.japanese: 仕事の後で、いっしょに飲みに行きませんか。
examples.english: Would you like to go for a drink after work?

examples.japanese: テストが終わった後で、友達と遊びました。
examples.english: After the test was over, I hung out with friends.

meaning: while (doing two actions at the same time)
usage: Both actions are done by the same person. The main action comes last: in A-ながら B, B is the main activity.

examples.japanese: 音楽を聞きながら勉強します。
examples.english: I study while listening to music.

examples.japanese: 父はいつも新聞を読みながら朝ご飯を食べます。
examples.english: My father always eats breakfast while reading the newspaper.

examples.japanese: コーヒーを飲みながら話しましょう。
examples.english: Let's talk over coffee.

structure: Verb-stem + に行く / Noun + に行く
usage: 来る and 帰る work the same way: 遊びに来る. With する-nouns the noun can come directly: 買い物に行く, 散歩に行く.

examples.japanese: デパートへ服を買いに行きます。
examples.english: I'm going to the department store to buy clothes.

examples.japanese: 週末、海へ泳ぎに行きました。
examples.english: I went to the beach to swim on the weekend.

examples.japanese: 友達がうちへ遊びに来ました。
examples.english: A friend came over to my place to hang out.

structure: Noun + が好き / Noun + が嫌い / Verb-dict + の + が好き
usage: 好き and 嫌い are な-adjectives, so the thing liked takes が, not を. 大好き and 大嫌い are stronger. 嫌い can sound blunt; あまり好きじゃない is softer.

examples.japanese: 私は甘いものが好きです。
examples.english: I like sweet things.

examples.japanese: 弟は野菜が嫌いです。
examples.english: My younger brother doesn't like vegetables.

examples.japanese: 母は料理をするのが好きです。
examples.english: My mother likes cooking.

structure: Noun + が上手 / Noun + が下手
usage: Mostly used about other people; calling yourself 上手 can sound like bragging. Both are な-adjectives: 料理が上手な人.

examples.japanese: 姉はピアノが上手です。
examples.english: My older sister is good at the piano.

examples.japanese: 私は歌が下手です。
examples.english: I'm bad at singing.

examples.japanese: マイクさんは日本語が上手ですね。
examples.english: Mike, your Japanese is really good.

meaning: there is; there are; have (ある for things, いる for people and animals)
structure: Noun + がある / Noun + がいる
usage: ある is for things, plants and events; いる is for people and animals. Negatives: ない / いない (polite: ありません / いません).

examples.japanese: 公園に大きい木があります。
examples.english: There is a big tree in the park.

examples.japanese: 私は妹が一人います。
examples.english: I have one younger sister.

examples.japanese: 明日、日本語のテストがあります。
examples.english: There's a Japanese test tomorrow.

usage: The reason comes first: A から B (A, so B). Answer どうして with 〜からです. Nouns and な-adjectives need だ: 雨だから.

examples.japanese: 今日は寒いから、コートを着ます。
examples.english: It's cold today, so I'll wear a coat.

examples.japanese: 時間がありませんから、タクシーで行きましょう。
examples.english: We don't have time, so let's take a taxi.

examples.japanese: 「どうして休みましたか。」「頭が痛かったからです。」
examples.english: "Why were you absent?" "Because I had a headache."

usage: Also used just to soften a request or lead into a topic: すみませんが…. A little more formal than けど (N4).

examples.japanese: この店は安いですが、あまりおいしくないです。
examples.english: This restaurant is cheap, but the food isn't very good.

examples.japanese: 日本語は難しいですが、おもしろいです。
examples.english: Japanese is difficult, but interesting.

examples.japanese: すみませんが、ちょっと静かにしてください。
examples.english: Excuse me, but please be a little quieter.

structure: Verb-plain / i-Adj / na-Adj / Noun + でしょう
usage: Typical of weather forecasts. Said with rising intonation, it asks the listener to agree. Plain form: だろう (N4).

examples.japanese: 明日は雨が降るでしょう。
examples.english: It will probably rain tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 山の上は寒いでしょう。
examples.english: It's probably cold at the top of the mountain.

examples.japanese: このかばん、かわいいでしょう？
examples.english: This bag is cute, isn't it?

structure: i-Adj-ku + なる / na-Adj + になる / Noun + になる
usage: いい becomes よくなる. Often used in the past to describe a change that has happened: 大きくなりました.

examples.japanese: あたたかくなりましたね。
examples.english: It's gotten warmer, hasn't it?

examples.japanese: 部屋がきれいになりました。
examples.english: The room has become clean.

examples.japanese: 兄は来年、医者になります。
examples.english: My older brother will become a doctor next year.

usage: Common when ordering food or picking from options. Past: 〜にしました (I decided on ...).

examples.japanese: 私はカレーにします。
examples.english: I'll have the curry.

examples.japanese: 飲み物は何にしますか。
examples.english: What would you like to drink?

examples.japanese: 旅行は来月にしましょう。
examples.english: Let's plan the trip for next month.

structure: まだ + Verb-te + いない / まだ + Verb-te + いません
usage: Use ていない, not ませんでした, for something that may still happen. The short answer is いいえ、まだです.

examples.japanese: まだ昼ご飯を食べていません。
examples.english: I haven't eaten lunch yet.

examples.japanese: 「宿題はもうしましたか。」「いいえ、まだしていません。」
examples.english: "Have you done your homework yet?" "No, not yet."

examples.japanese: 電車はまだ来ていません。
examples.english: The train hasn't come yet.

structure: もう + Verb-ta / もう + Verb-stem + ました
usage: In questions もう means 'yet'. With a negative verb, もう means 'no longer': もう食べません.

examples.japanese: 「もう晩ご飯を食べましたか。」「はい、もう食べました。」
examples.english: "Have you eaten dinner yet?" "Yes, I already have."

examples.japanese: 妹はもう寝ました。
examples.english: My younger sister has already gone to bed.

examples.japanese: 映画はもう始まりましたよ。
examples.english: The movie has already started.

meaning: not very; not much; not often
structure: あまり + Verb-nai / あまり + i-Adj-ku + ない / あまり + na-Adj + じゃない
usage: Always followed by a negative form. あまり好きじゃない is a softer way to say you dislike something.

examples.japanese: 私はあまりテレビを見ません。
examples.english: I don't watch much TV.

examples.japanese: このりんごはあまり甘くないです。
examples.english: This apple isn't very sweet.

examples.japanese: 今日はあまり忙しくありません。
examples.english: I'm not very busy today.

meaning: not at all; not in the least
structure: 全然 + Verb-nai / 全然 + i-Adj-ku + ない / 全然 + na-Adj + じゃない
usage: Stronger than あまり〜ない. In casual speech 全然 is sometimes used with positive words (全然大丈夫), but with a negative is the standard use.

examples.japanese: この問題は全然わかりません。
examples.english: I don't understand this question at all.

examples.japanese: 今日は全然寒くないです。
examples.english: It's not cold at all today.

examples.japanese: 弟は全然勉強しません。
examples.english: My younger brother doesn't study at all.

structure: Noun + だけ / Verb-dict + だけ
usage: Neutral in tone. Compare しか〜ない (N4), which stresses that the amount is small.

examples.japanese: 財布に100円だけあります。
examples.english: I only have 100 yen in my wallet.

examples.japanese: 朝はコーヒーだけ飲みます。
examples.english: In the morning I only have coffee.

examples.japanese: 日曜日だけ休みです。
examples.english: Sunday is my only day off.

meaning: about; approximately (an amount or length of time)
structure: Noun + くらい / Noun + ぐらい
usage: Used with amounts and durations. For a point in time (around three o'clock), use ごろ: 3時ごろ.

examples.japanese: 駅まで歩いて10分ぐらいです。
examples.english: It's about a ten-minute walk to the station.

examples.japanese: 毎日2時間くらい勉強します。
examples.english: I study for about two hours every day.

examples.japanese: このかばんは5000円ぐらいでした。
examples.english: This bag was about 5,000 yen.

usage: Attaches to clock times, dates and months. に after ごろ is optional: 7時ごろ(に)起きます.

examples.japanese: 毎晩11時ごろ寝ます。
examples.english: I go to bed around eleven every night.

examples.japanese: 4月ごろ、桜が咲きます。
examples.english: The cherry blossoms bloom around April.

examples.japanese: 夕方6時ごろに家に帰ります。
examples.english: I get home around six in the evening.

pattern: 何も〜ない / 誰も〜ない
meaning: nothing; nobody; not anything; not anyone
structure: 何も + Verb-nai / 誰も + Verb-nai
usage: With places, a particle comes before も: どこにも / どこへも行きません (go nowhere). 誰 is often written in hiragana: だれ.

examples.japanese: けさは何も食べませんでした。
examples.english: I didn't eat anything this morning.

examples.japanese: 教室にはだれもいません。
examples.english: There's nobody in the classroom.

examples.japanese: 冷蔵庫の中には何もありません。
examples.english: There's nothing in the fridge.

pattern: 何か / 誰か / どこか
usage: Question word + か gives 'some-' words; question word + も + negative gives 'no-' words. が and を after 何か / だれか are often dropped.

examples.japanese: 何か飲みますか。
examples.english: Would you like something to drink?

examples.japanese: だれか来ましたよ。
examples.english: Someone's here.

examples.japanese: 夏休みにどこかへ行きましたか。
examples.english: Did you go anywhere during summer vacation?

pattern: これ / それ / あれ / どれ
meaning: this one; that one (near you); that one (over there); which one
structure: これ / それ / あれ / どれ
usage: こ = near the speaker, そ = near the listener, あ = away from both, ど = question. They stand alone; as a subject どれ takes が, not は.

examples.japanese: これは私の辞書です。
examples.english: This is my dictionary.

examples.japanese: それは何ですか。
examples.english: What is that?

examples.japanese: 「あなたのかさはどれですか。」「あれです。」
examples.english: "Which one is your umbrella?" "That one over there."

pattern: この / その / あの / どの
meaning: this; that (near you); that ... over there; which (before a noun)
structure: この / その / あの / どの + Noun
usage: Always followed by a noun: この本, never この alone. これ / それ / あれ / どれ are used when there is no noun.

examples.japanese: このケーキはおいしいです。
examples.english: This cake is delicious.

examples.japanese: その本はだれのですか。
examples.english: Whose book is that?

examples.japanese: 「どの人が先生ですか。」「あの人です。」
examples.english: "Which person is the teacher?" "That person over there."

pattern: ここ / そこ / あそこ / どこ
meaning: here; there (near you); over there; where
structure: ここ / そこ / あそこ / どこ
usage: こちら / そちら / あちら / どちら are politer versions: お国はどちらですか (Where are you from?).

examples.japanese: ここは私の学校です。
examples.english: This is my school.

examples.japanese: トイレはあそこです。
examples.english: The restroom is over there.

examples.japanese: すみません、駅はどこですか。
examples.english: Excuse me, where is the station?

meaning: negative and past forms of i-adjectives (is not; was; was not)
structure: i-Adj stem + くない / i-Adj stem + かった / i-Adj stem + くなかった
usage: 高い→高くない, 高かった, 高くなかった. Add です to be polite. いい is irregular: よくない, よかった, よくなかった.

examples.japanese: この部屋はあまり広くないです。
examples.english: This room isn't very big.

examples.japanese: きのうのテストは難しかったです。
examples.english: Yesterday's test was difficult.

examples.japanese: 先週見た映画はおもしろくなかったです。
examples.english: The movie I saw last week wasn't interesting.

meaning: na-adjectives: take な before a noun and です or だ at the end of a sentence
structure: na-Adj + な + Noun / na-Adj + です / na-Adj + ではありません / na-Adj + でした
usage: Before a noun, add な: 静かな部屋. At the end of a sentence they change like nouns. きれい and きらい end in い but are な-adjectives.

examples.japanese: 京都は有名な町です。
examples.english: Kyoto is a famous city.

examples.japanese: きのうは暇でした。
examples.english: I was free yesterday.

examples.japanese: この部屋はあまり静かではありません。
examples.english: This room isn't very quiet.

structure: i-Adj-ku + て / na-Adj + で / Noun + で
usage: いい becomes よくて. Join qualities that point the same way (both good or both bad); for a contrast, use が instead.

examples.japanese: この店は安くておいしいです。
examples.english: This restaurant is cheap and good.

examples.japanese: 私の町は静かできれいです。
examples.english: My town is quiet and clean.

examples.japanese: 兄は大学生で、妹は高校生です。
examples.english: My older brother is a university student, and my younger sister is a high school student.

usage: Introduces a name the listener may not know.

examples.japanese: これは「すきやき」という料理です。
examples.english: This is a dish called sukiyaki.

examples.japanese: 「さくら」という店でアルバイトをしています。
examples.english: I work part-time at a shop called Sakura.

examples.japanese: 山田さんという人から電話がありました。
examples.english: There was a call from someone named Yamada.
